title: Reading the owner's vision against the repository, and choosing what to build first
request: Read my earlier conversations about this R&D project in full (a 17-page question list and a 40-page transcript) and understand everything I want to build. The closest product is Hugging Face's ML Intern, for most kinds of machine-learning projects. Do not change code; review it carefully.
spec: A review in English and Persian: the vision restated in the owner's terms, each idea mapped to what the repository already has and what is missing, and a prioritized order toward an MVP, ending with one proposal for what to build next. No code changes.
plan: Read every page of both documents before answering.
Restate the product in one sentence and in six layers: the evidence engine, the workflow engine (WF-01 to WF-10), the agent surfaces, a focused small model, cost efficiency, domain packs.
Map each layer to the repository with a status: built, partial, missing, or waiting on the owner.
Name the two biggest gaps against ML Intern.
Propose an order for the MVP, with the reason the first step comes first.
Give the same review in Persian and ask which step to start.

decisions.decision: Frame DCLab's edge over ML Intern as being right, not only automatic: contract before any score, leakage caught, holdout once, every suggestion linked to evidence.
decisions.why: That is what the R&D measured and what a general agent does not offer; it also decides what to build first.

decisions.decision: Report the workflow graph as only partial although the five stages already run in order.
decisions.why: The stages only enforced 'run the previous stage first'; there were no explicit allowed moves, no stop, ask or go-back moves, and moves were not logged as training data.

decisions.decision: Name two biggest gaps: no real code execution, and no measured proof that the agent judges well.
decisions.why: Covering most kinds of ML needs sandboxed code and GPU jobs; and without a benchmark 'DCLab is right' is a claim, not evidence.

decisions.decision: Recommend the workflow graph and its validator as step 1, then a judgment benchmark, sandboxed execution, a first non-tabular pack, the policy model, and later research (macro-tokens, the cost ladder, speculative decoding).
decisions.why: The graph is small and deterministic, everything after it depends on it, and its logged moves are the trajectory data the small model needs.

decisions.decision: Keep macro-tokens (a whole step as one token) as a separate research question.
decisions.why: It is unmeasured; the policy model can be built and measured without it.

decisions.decision: Ask the owner for about ten minutes on the prediction-moment worksheet for HyperAck and churn, in parallel.
decisions.why: Only the owner knows the prediction moment, and it decides which HyperAck champion counts as safe.

change: No code changed: a written review with a status table (evidence engine built; notebook with five stages built, tabular only; intern built; Chat UI over MCP built and tested; SFT data ready but no training run; workflow graph partial; judgment benchmark only the 6 of 7 pilot; code execution and GPU jobs missing; domain packs beyond tabular missing; cost ladder partial; VS Code companion partial; owner worksheet waiting).
outcome: Delivered. The owner then asked for a clickable demo of the final product (PRE-product-demo) and the graph and its validator were built next (PRE-workflow-graph), as the review recommended.
lessons: Before planning, map every idea to what exists with an honest status; a stage order that runs is not yet a controlled graph.
Choose the first step by dependency: build the small deterministic piece that every later piece needs and that produces the data they learn from.
Separate measured capability from claims: list a benchmark as a gap until it exists.
risks: Answering from a skim of the 17-page question list and the 40-page transcript, and restating a vision the owner does not hold.
Marking a layer as built because code exists, when it only runs in a fixed order (the five stages) or only on tabular data.
Recommending a first step that later steps do not depend on, so the roadmap has to be reordered after work has started.
Counting the small notebook pilot as a judgment benchmark, which would hide the biggest gap against ML Intern.
Changing code during a review that was asked to leave the code untouched.
